source.title: Infinity∞: Scaling Bitwise AutoRegressive Modeling for High-Resolution Image Synthesis
source.authors: Jian Han; Jinlai Liu; Yi Jiang; Bin Yan; Yu-Qi Zhang; Zehuan Yuan; Bing-Yue Peng; Xiaobing Liu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling in visual autoregressive image generation and reports a relationship between validation loss and image-generation evaluation metrics, extending scaling-related measurements to a different modality.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws but does not test language models. Its own relevant results are the Infinity visual-model scaling sweep and validation-loss correlations in Section 4.5. Other benchmark comparisons and the tokenizer-vocabulary and self-correction ablations do not measure the claim versions' named outcomes.
record.test_reason: Section 4.5 scales a visual autoregressive text-to-image model from 125M to 4.7B parameters. It reports validation loss falling with size and compute, plus Pearson correlations between validation loss and three image-generation metrics. That is a new-modality result on downstream predictability (V6) and a qualitative, unfitted result on scaling beyond text (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report that validation loss decreases smoothly with model size and training compute, and that it correlates nearly linearly with GenEval, ImageReward and HPSv2 across 125M–4.7B models. They take this to encourage further scaling. The paper's overall conclusion concerns Infinity's generation quality and speed.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a visual autoregressive image-generation model and measures validation loss and image metrics; it does not reproduce the language-model loss measurements or compute-optimal fitting methods of the cited work.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models trained for fewer steps reach lower validation loss than smaller models trained longer at comparable compute (Fig. 10). The authors say this aligns with language-model findings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute efficiency favours larger models in visual autoregressive generation (qualitative, no fixed-compute optimum fitted).

fits_no_version.finding: The better tokenizer vocabulary size depends on model size: 2^16 is better for 125M/361M, while 2^32 beats 2^16 at 2.2B after 40K iterations (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal tokenizer vocabulary size grows with transformer size in visual AR models.

record.peer_reviewed: preprint; the paper text says it is under review
record.problems: The scaling loss curves are presented in a figure without numerical loss values; no power-law fit, uncertainty estimate, or small-run extrapolation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the listed versions were found. The text cites language-model scaling laws but reports no results for those cited studies.

untested.parts: Whether visual-model loss follows a power law, and its exponents. Only a smooth decrease is described, with no fit. Other modalities and regimes (video, repeated data, fine-tuning) are not tested.
Prediction of larger-run downstream performance from small runs. Downstream measures other than GenEval, ImageReward and HPSv2. Language-model tasks.
Not tested: no language-model loss is measured.
Not tested: there is no extrapolation from fitted small runs.
Not tested: there is no fixed-compute sweep over parameters and tokens.
Not tested: depth and width co-vary with size (Table 6), with no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Not tested: no exponents are fitted or compared.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The scaling analysis is secondary to a method paper. It has no power-law fits, no numerical loss values and no uncertainty; the correlations come from five points. The V6 support therefore sits in a narrow setting, image generation at 256px.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws in language models.
No power law fitted on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architectures at fixed parameter count.

The paper measures visual-model validation loss as model size and training compute increase, but does not fit or test whether the relationship has the same power-law form or exponents as text pretraining. It does not test the other listed modalities or regimes.
The reported downstream measures are image-generation evaluation metrics (GenEval, ImageReward, HPSv2); other downstream tasks and language-model performance are not tested.
The paper does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across setups or fitting choices, or report curves bending away from a power law.
